html:
The Phoenician cities were trading city-states on the coast of the Levant, mostly in today's Lebanon, that dominated sea trade in the Mediterranean from about 1200 BCE until the Persians took them over in 539 BCE. The chief cities were Tyre, Sidon, Byblos and Arwad.

The Phoenicians were Canaanites who spoke a Semitic language. After the collapse of the Bronze Age powers around 1200 BCE, they filled the gap left in sea trade. They were never one state; each city had its own king and often competed with the others.

What they traded:

  • Cedar wood from the mountains of Lebanon, sought by Egypt and Mesopotamia.
  • Cloth dyed with Tyrian purple, made from sea snails and so costly it became the colour of kings.
  • Glass, carved ivory, metalwork and wine.

They sailed further than anyone else of their time and planted colonies and trading posts across the Mediterranean, in Cyprus, Sicily, Sardinia and Spain. They founded Gadir, today's Cádiz, beyond the Strait of Gibraltar, and Tyre founded Carthage, which later outgrew its mother city.

Their most lasting gift was the Phoenician alphabet of 22 letters, which traders carried to the Greeks and which is the ancestor of most alphabets in use today.

The cities paid tribute to Assyria, and Tyre held out for thirteen years against a siege by Nebuchadnezzar II of Babylon. In 539 BCE they passed to the Persian Empire, whose navy they largely supplied, until Alexander took Tyre in 332 BCE.
